text.short: One city block in Boise carries more Basque life than any other address in the United States — a museum in a boarding house, a bar, a market, a dining room, a club, and a festival that brings 30,000 people every five years.

sections.heading: The Basque Block
sections.body: Grove Street between Sixth and Capitol. A pub, a market, a dining room with a hotel over it, the Basque Center, and the museum — inside the boarding house the museum grew out of. Nowhere else in America concentrates the whole apparatus on one block.

sections.heading: The building the rest of this site is about
sections.body: Cyrus Jacobs put up a brick house on Grove Street in 1864. It became a Basque boarding house; the Uberuaga family ran it from 1917, bought it in 1928, and kept taking boarders until 1969. Adelia Simplot bought it from them and opened the Basque Museum & Cultural Center in it in 1985 — the first museum in the country given to Basque history. Every long table in California and Nevada descends from a room like that one, and this is the room still standing.

sections.heading: Jaialdi
sections.body: Every five years Boise holds Jaialdi, six days, 30,000 to 50,000 people. The last one ran 29 July to 3 August 2025. The next is 2030.

sections.heading: And outside Boise
sections.body: Meridian has a family restaurant founded in 1999 by the descendants of a woman born in Bizkaia in 1903. Sweet, population small, has an inn that opens Friday to Sunday. Idaho's Basque country is not only a city block.
